questions.problem: Write the complex number $z=-2+6\text{i}$ in the form $r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ giving $\theta $ in radians to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
To write our complex number in the form $z=r{\text{e}}^{\text{i}\theta },$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z),$ we first calculate $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{6}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z$ lies in the second quadrant of the complex plane, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-3)| \\  & ≈1.893.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $r=2\sqrt{10}$ and $\theta =1.893$ into $z=r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ we get

$$
z=2\sqrt{10}\,{\text{e}}^{1.893\,\text{i}}.
$$

questions.problem: Write the complex number $z=1+2\text{i}$ in the form $r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ giving $\theta $ in radians to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
To write $z$ in the form $z=r{\text{e}}^{\text{i}\theta },$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z),$ we first calculate $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z$ lies in the first quadrant of the complex plane, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{2}{1}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2) \\  & ≈1.107.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $r=\sqrt{5}$ and $\theta =1.107$ into $z=r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ we get

$$
z=\sqrt{5}\,{\text{e}}^{1.107\,\text{i}}.
$$

questions.problem: Write the complex number $z=5-\text{i}$ in the form $r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ giving $\theta $ in radians to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
To write our complex number in the form $z=r{\text{e}}^{\text{i}\theta },$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z),$ we first calculate $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{26}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $z$ lies in the fourth quadrant, we can find the angle $\theta $ as

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =2\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =2\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{-1}{5})| \\  & =2\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\frac{1}{5})| \\  & ≈2\pi -0.197\,39… \\  & ≈6.086.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $r=\sqrt{26}$ and $\theta =6.086$ into $z=r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ we get

$$
z=\sqrt{26}\,{\text{e}}^{6.086\,\text{i}}.
$$

questions.problem: Write the complex number $z=-1+\text{i}$ in exponential form.
questions.worked_solution:
To write our complex number in the form $z=r{\text{e}}^{\text{i}\theta },$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z),$ we first calculate $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{(1)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $z$ lies in the second quadrant, we can find the angle $\theta $ as

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =\pi -|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-1)| \\  & =\pi -\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $r=\sqrt{2}$ and $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{4}$ into $z=r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ we get 

$$
z=\sqrt{2}\,{\text{e}}^{3\pi \text{i}/4}.

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{(2\sqrt{3})}^{2}} \\  & =4\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Finally, substituting $r=4$ and $\theta =\frac{2\pi }{3}$ into $z=r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ we get

Write the complex number $z$, shown on the Argand diagram above, in exponential form.
questions.worked_solution:
The complex number shown in the Argand diagram can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =x+\text{i}y \\  & =-\sqrt{3}-\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

To write it in the form $z=r{\text{e}}^{\text{i}\theta },$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z),$ we first calculate $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(-\sqrt{3})}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $z$ lies in the third quadrant, we can find the angle $\theta $ as

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\pi +|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})| \\  & =\pi +|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{-1}{-\sqrt{3}})| \\  & =\pi +|\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})| \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $r=2$ and $\theta =\frac{7\pi }{6}$ into $z=r{e}^{\text{i}\theta },$ we get 

$$
z=2\,{\text{e}}^{7\pi \text{i}/6}.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Write the complex number $z=4+4\textrm{i}$ in exponential form.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To write our complex number in the form $z = r\textrm{e}^{\textrm{i}\theta},$ where $r=|z|$ and $\theta = \arg(z),$ we first calculate $r\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z$ lies in the first quadrant of the complex plane, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting $r=4\sqrt{2}$ and $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ into $z=re^{\textrm{i}\theta},$ we get

$$
z = 4\sqrt{2}\,\textrm{e}^{\pi\textrm{i}/4}.
$$
